item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I like the concept of an item that has gone from being a weapon, to a fuel source to a liability because the world changed while it did not, quite a lot. I also think this used the format very aptly to tell its story. I am willing to suspend disbelief that the 3rd century records could be arranged to fit in this format, but I would prefer a Latin name and period organizational structure. I think I am weakly upvoting, but would be much more enthusiastic if Darke Co. was something more appropriate.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: That final note isn't much of a 'gotcha' or twist. That said, I liked this more than the last MC&D I saw, and it's entirely because you were able to tell a story economically via e-mails, rather than sequentially.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I think "Trading Co." is anachronistic, and so is the concept of guilds (it's Medieval). If we're looking at the era (Roman Empire), perhaps a hidden forum (my suggestion: Forum Tenebris, Forum Plutus) would be more suitable.

Can't really use "Dark", since the name is at least Germanic in origin. I don't think Germanic tribes are involved in Roman trade during the Imperial era.

Alternatively, check out the Merchants' entry in the Wanderers' Library.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I did change the name from MC&D Ltd. to reflect them existing before the modern concept of corporations. Darke does fit the description of a wealthy individual/family. Though 'Trading Co.' might not be the most accurate term (guild, perhaps?), I did want to communicate that it's more than a one-person operation.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Your crosslink is currently broken.

As for the rest of it… it doesn't particularly do much for me. It's a fair exploration of the consequences of a petroleum-producing object through the ages, but the events of the narrative never break out and go anywhere particularly interesting. No vote.

Also, I'm not an expert, but "The Darke Trading Co." is pretty anachronistic for the Romans circa 264. Joint stock companies didn't exist until the 14th century at the earliest. I usually see mention of trade at the time either focusing on wealthy individuals/families or operations run by the state (e.g. grain cultivation and transport for the grain dole), or state contractors such as the publicans. (Possible further details in this article on Roman commerce.) It's not that I don't see a place for a Darke organization in Rome. Given the prodigious trade and incredible wealth/class gap it makes perfect sense. I'm just saying it wouldn't be, or particularly look like, a Co.

But, again, I'm not an expert. History's purely a hobby thing for me.
